If I had to choose one thing to write about freely, I would choose the strange beauty of ordinary moments.

There is a kind of quiet magic in the parts of life we usually overlook: the sound of rain tapping against a window, the way steam rises from a cup of tea, the pause between one thought and the next. We spend so much time waiting for large, dramatic events — successes, disasters, transformations — but most of life is made of small, unremarkable seconds. And yet those seconds are where we actually live.

I think people underestimate how much courage it takes to notice. To really notice the world means to slow down, to let yourself be moved by something simple, to admit that a stretch of sunlight on a wall can matter. Attention is a gentle act of rebellion against distraction.

Maybe that is why writing — or any kind of creation — feels important. It tries to preserve what is always passing. It says: this happened, I saw it, it mattered. Not because it was enormous, but because it was real.

So if I can write about anything, I want to write about the ordinary made luminous. The way a familiar street can suddenly look beautiful in the evening. The way a stranger’s laugh can linger. The way being alive is both incredibly fragile and strangely persistent.

In the end, I think wonder is not reserved for rare occasions. It is available constantly, hidden in plain sight, waiting for us to be still enough to find it.
